title: The Checkout Lane Is Designed to Break You
editorialNotes: The 40-100% register markup and retailer slow-checkout claims have no entry in the Notion source index; carried as body copy only, never hero type.

thread.element: checkout lane with a circled impulse zone moving toward the register
thread.endState: every trick zone circled on one lane

copy.headline: The checkout lane is a trap. Here's how it works.
The hunger window.
items: Most people grocery shop after work or before dinner — when they're hungry.
Checkout candy, chips, and drinks are placed at eye level for adults and grab level for kids.
This isn't convenience. It's behavioral targeting.

copy.headline: The wait tax.
copy.body: Long lines aren't always understaffing. Some retailers intentionally slow checkout to increase dwell time near impulse products. Self-checkout is faster — but notice how the candy is still there.

copy.headline: Magazine and gum placement.
items: Low-margin, high-impulse items are placed where you stand still.
You've already committed to the purchase mentally by being in line. Adding $3 feels like nothing against a $120 cart.

copy.headline: The "cold case" near checkout.
copy.body: Drinks at the register are marked up 40–100% compared to the beverage aisle. Same brand. Same size. Different price. You're paying for proximity and thirst.

copy.headline: The small cart illusion.
items: Some stores introduced smaller carts to seem eco-friendly.
Others made carts larger over the last decade.
Bigger cart = your haul looks smaller = you buy more to "fill" it.

copy.headline: Every aisle is a funnel. The store profits when you overbuy and overwaste.
copy.ctaLine: fond helps you track what you actually have — so you only buy what you need. Link in bio.
